title: The Merger
logline: Meridian buys Lumen, and Marcus must merge two platforms, two teams and two ways of working while Lumen's architect, Victor Hale, competes for the same job.

modules.logline: Marcus inherits Lumen's Scala, JVM and Kubernetes estate and must learn to read it before he can judge it.
scenes: Launch night ends at 4 a.m.: traffic fails over to the second region and Lena closes the incident. At nine, Asha announces Meridian is buying Lumen. Victor Hale's estate runs on the JVM. Why should a Python engineer care?

Victor shares a repository and says nothing. Marcus opens it: case classes, Options, pattern matches, a for-comprehension over Futures. Lena says it looks like Python wearing armour. Can Marcus read Scala well enough to review it by Friday?

Lumen's nightly fare job is a Spark Scala pipeline of typed Datasets and a few UDFs. Victor calls it faster than anything Meridian runs. Marcus spots a map over every row. Is it really faster, or just harder to read?

At 2 a.m. the Lumen fare job dies with an OutOfMemoryError. Lena, now leading on-call, pages Marcus. The executor heap looks fine, yet the container was killed anyway. Two kinds of out-of-memory, one alert. Which one is this?

Lumen runs Spark and Flink for forty teams on one shared Kubernetes cluster. Pods sit Pending all morning while one team's job hogs the nodes. Victor shrugs: requests and limits are the teams' problem. Are they, on a platform?

In a corner of Lumen's estate sits a Hadoop cluster: YARN queues, Hive tables, eight years of ride history. Victor wants it gone in a quarter. Dev wants it left alone. What does a safe migration off Hadoop look like?
teasers: Victor sends a Scala repository and a Friday deadline. Can Marcus review it in time?
Victor says Python could never keep up with Lumen's fare job. Is Scala faster, or just harder to read?
A 2 a.m. page: the JVM runs out of memory where nobody looks. Heap, metaspace or off-heap?
Forty teams share one cluster and pods will not schedule. Are they platform users or tenants?
Eight years of rides sit on a forgotten Hadoop cluster. What does a safe migration look like?
Next week: Databricks and Snowflake, one set of tables. How does Delta decide which files to skip?
modules.boss: Saturday's review: the Lumen fare job that died at 2 a.m. Victor blames Meridian's data volume; Marcus suspects off-heap memory. Lena chairs. Read the Scala, the GC logs and the pod events, then decide who is right.
modules.finale: Marcus approves Victor's pull request with three comments, all correct. Victor replies with one word: fair. Grace says, 'Learn their stack before you judge it.' Then finance asks why the same trips table exists twice, in Databricks and Snowflake.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "What did you build today?" Marcus: "Nothing new; I learned to read another team's language so I can help the people who wrote in it."

modules.logline: Lumen's Databricks and Meridian's Snowflake must serve one set of tables, and one rider's deletion request tests whether either can.
scenes: Merger day thirty. Lumen's analysts live in Databricks notebooks; Meridian's finance team lives in Snowflake. Mei finds both platforms storing the same trips and billing for both. Tom asks why there are two. Is either team wrong?

Victor walks Marcus through a Delta table: Parquet files, a _delta_log of JSON commits, a checkpoint every ten. One query scans four thousand tiny files. How does Delta decide which files to skip, and why is it skipping so few?

Marcus returns the favour in Snowflake: micro-partitions, clustering, a warehouse that suspends after sixty seconds. Victor's query runs in eight seconds here, but bills credits by the second. Which engine prunes better, and which is cheaper per answer?

Asha wants one copy of trips, readable from both engines. Victor proposes Delta with UniForm; Marcus suggests Iceberg tables that Snowflake can read. Both plans dodge the same question. Who owns the writes when two engines share one table?

A rider in Bengaluru emails support: delete my data, everywhere. Her trips live in Delta, in Snowflake and in three old snapshots. Legal gives thirty days. Deleting a row is easy. How does Marcus prove it is gone from history too?

Lumen tags support tickets with a language model inside a nightly batch job. It is cheap until a failure makes it retry every row. Victor wants it in Snowflake next. Should a model sit inside a pipeline, and on which platform?
teasers: Victor opens a Delta log. Why is Delta skipping so few files?
The same query runs on both engines. Which prunes better, and which is cheaper per answer?
Asha wants one copy read by two engines. Who owns the writes?
A rider asks to be deleted everywhere within thirty days. How do you prove it is gone from history?
A model in a batch pipeline bills for every retry. Should it sit inside the pipeline at all?
Next week: 12% of Lumen's rows vanish and every job is green. Which test would have caught it?
modules.boss: The weekend review: the rider deletion. Support says it is done; an auditor finds her trips in a Delta time-travel version and a Snowflake clone. Walk through vacuum, retention, clones and masking, and show where the process leaked.
modules.finale: One trips table, two engines, and a deletion runbook legal signs. Victor admits Snowflake's pruning surprised him. Grace says, 'Two tools is fine; two truths is not.' Then on Monday the trip count drops 12% overnight.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why do you need two computers to hold the same toys?" Marcus: "We don't; we are teaching both of them to share one toy box."

Recall: Should a model sit inside a pipeline, and on which platform?

modules.logline: When 12% of rows vanish without a single failed job, Marcus and Lena build tests, contracts and write-audit-publish so failures can no longer hide.
scenes: Monday standup. Every Airflow task is green, yet the Lumen trips table holds 12% fewer rows than on Friday. Tom's dashboard already shows a dip in Chennai demand. Nothing failed. How does a pipeline lose data while reporting success?

Lena traces the loss to an inner join against a driver table that arrived late. No test checked row counts. Victor says Lumen tests in production. Marcus asks which tests would have caught this, and where they should run.

The driver table belongs to a Lumen partner team, who renamed a column last Thursday without telling anyone. Victor calls it their right. Marcus calls it a broken promise. What would a data contract between the teams actually say?

Dev proposes a rule: no table is published until it is audited. Victor worries it doubles storage and slows every job. Marcus sketches write, audit, publish on a staging branch. Can bad data wait there without consumers noticing the delay?

Asha asks for one health dashboard: freshness, volume, schema and distribution. Lena adds CI that runs the tests on every pull request. Then a harmless rename passes CI and breaks a Snowflake view. What did the checks not see?

At 3 a.m. Lena runs an incident herself, calm, with a clear timeline in Slack. Afterwards she asks Marcus for an on-call agent that reads Airflow failures and gathers evidence. How much should an agent diagnose before a human looks?
teasers: The missing rows hide behind an untested join. Which tests would have caught it, and where?
A partner team renamed a column and told nobody. What would a data contract say?
Dev wants nothing published before an audit. Can bad data wait without consumers noticing?
A health dashboard stays green while a view breaks. What did the checks not see?
Lena leads a 3 a.m. incident alone. How much should an agent diagnose before a person looks?
Next week: ten times the traffic and a lost region. Do Marcus's numbers survive Mei's questions?
modules.boss: The weekend review: 12% of rows vanished and nobody was paged. Lena presents the timeline. Find the root cause, the missing contract, the test that should exist, and where write-audit-publish would have stopped the bad load.
modules.finale: The contract is signed, the audit step blocks bad loads, and Lena's postmortem is the clearest Marcus has read. Victor copies it for Lumen. Grace says, 'Make the failure loud before you make it rare.' Then Asha books a design review.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "How do you know all the toys are there?" Marcus: "We count them before anyone plays, and if some are missing, the box stays shut."

Recall: What would a data contract between the teams actually say?

Recall: How much should an agent diagnose before a human looks?

modules.logline: Asha asks for a design that survives ten times the traffic and a lost region, and Marcus and Victor must design it out loud together.
scenes: Asha books a design review: the combined company expects ten times the trips within two years. Marcus and Victor each get forty-five minutes at the whiteboard. Victor starts drawing at once. Marcus starts with questions. Which approach does the room trust?

Marcus does the arithmetic aloud: two hundred million events a day, about two thousand a second, peaks ten times higher on festival nights. Mei asks what a year of storage costs. Do his numbers hold up under her questions?

The rider app needs a trip's fare in under fifty milliseconds. Victor proposes reading straight from Delta. Dev suggests a key-value store. Kofi wants Snowflake. Three serving stores, one latency budget. Which one fits the access pattern?

Victor asks what happens when two regions accept the same payment update. Marcus reaches for quorum, idempotency keys and exactly-once. Lena asks which of those words actually stops a double charge. Can Marcus explain it plainly?

Asha calls a surprise drill: the primary region is gone, now. Traffic doubles elsewhere, Kafka lag climbs, warehouse loads stall. Marcus and Victor share one whiteboard and ten minutes. What fails first, and what do they shed?

Lena brings a pipeline an AI assistant wrote for the drill: tidy, documented, and wrong in two places. Victor finds one, Marcus the other. What mistakes does AI-written pipeline code make, and how should a reviewer hunt for them?
teasers: Marcus estimates ten times scale out loud. Do his numbers survive Mei's questions?
Three serving stores and a fifty-millisecond budget for one fare. Which fits the access pattern?
Two regions accept the same payment. Can Marcus explain consistency in plain words?
Asha switches off a region mid-review. What fails first, and what do you shed?
An AI-written pipeline looks perfect and is wrong twice. How should a reviewer hunt the mistakes?
Next week: Victor wants every domain to own its data. What makes something a data product?
modules.boss: The weekend round: the lost-region drill, replayed. Ten times the traffic, one region dark, Kafka lag rising. Clarify, estimate, draw, go deep, break it and scale it, in forty-five minutes, as Marcus and Victor did.
modules.finale: The drill ends with no lost payments and a one-page design both names sign. Asha calls it the first document from the merged team. Grace says, 'Draw the failure first.' Then Victor sends a memo proposing data mesh for everyone.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "What if the big computer room loses power?" Marcus: "Another room in another city takes over, and we practise that before it ever happens."
recall: Recall: Which approach does the room trust?
Recall: Do his numbers hold up under her questions?
Recall: Which one fits the access pattern?
Recall: Can Marcus explain it plainly?
Recall: What fails first, and what do they shed?
Recall: What mistakes does AI-written pipeline code make, and how should a reviewer hunt for them?

modules.logline: Victor's push for data mesh forces Marcus to decide which domains should own their data products and which still need a central team.
scenes: Victor's memo lands in every inbox: dissolve the central data team and give each domain its own data. Kofi's analysts worry. Dev calls it a reorganisation dressed as architecture. Why does data mesh exist, and what problem does it solve?

Asha asks for one example before any reorganisation. Marcus picks the trips dataset: an owner, a contract, SLOs, a catalogue entry, a stable interface. Lena asks what makes it a product rather than a table with a nice name.

The payments domain refuses: two engineers, no data skills, a quarter-end audit coming. Victor says ownership is non-negotiable. Marcus suspects mesh is the wrong answer for some teams. How does he decide which domains are ready?

If every domain builds its own pipelines, who runs storage, access and quality checks? Marcus sketches a self-serve platform; Victor adds policies enforced as code. Dev asks who wins when a domain's rule conflicts with the central one.

The trips product launches. Three weeks later, two teams use it and five still query the old warehouse copy. Kofi will not switch until it matches his numbers. How do you move consumers off a central warehouse without breaking them?

Victor shows Lumen's earlier mesh attempt: forty data products, eleven owners who have left, nine with no consumers. He wants it done properly this time. Marcus asks which failure modes companies hit, and which ones they are already repeating.
teasers: Asha wants one real data product before any reorg. What makes it a product, not a table?
Payments refuses to own its data and Victor will not budge. Which domains are ready?
Domains want independence and Dev asks who sets the rules. Who runs the shared platform?
The trips product is live and Kofi still queries the old copy. How do consumers move safely?
Victor opens a graveyard of forty abandoned data products. Which failure modes are they repeating?
Next week: Dev's template is six weeks old and unused. Which journey should be paved first?
modules.boss: The weekend review: Victor's mesh proposal, as Asha will hear it on Monday. Name which domains own data products, write one product spec with an owner, a contract and an SLO, and say where mesh is the wrong answer.
modules.finale: Three domains own products; payments stays central for now. Victor calls it half a mesh. Marcus calls it the half that works. Grace says, 'Move ownership only where someone wants it.' Then Dev's new template sits unused.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Who owns the toys?" Marcus: "Whoever plays with them most looks after them, and promises to keep them tidy for everyone else."

modules.logline: Dev's pipeline templates sit unused until Marcus and Victor learn to build golden paths that teams choose rather than obey.
scenes: Dev's pipeline template has been live six weeks with zero users. Lumen teams copy Victor's old Scala scaffold instead. Dev wants to mandate the template. Marcus wants to know why nobody chose it. What is a golden path, really?

Marcus lists how teams actually ship: a new batch pipeline, a data product, a backfill, a stream. Lena times each one: eleven days for a new pipeline. Victor says pave everything. Which journey should they pave first?

Lena drafts the template: Airflow DAG, dbt models, tests, owner tag, alerts and cost labels, all on by default. Victor asks how a team escapes when it needs something different. What belongs in a template, and what stays optional?

Two months later, thirty pipelines built from the template run three different versions of it. A security fix reaches only nine. Dev sighs that templates always rot. How do you keep a template alive after teams copy it?

Kofi's team wants to skip platform review, which takes a week. Victor proposes a developer portal with one-click creation. Marcus proposes CI checks instead of the review meeting. Can guardrails replace a gate without letting risk through?

Asha asks whether the golden path works. Dev shows downloads. Marcus shows time to first pipeline, down from eleven days to one. Victor shows the teams that left it. Which number proves teams actually chose the road?
teasers: A new pipeline takes eleven days. Which journey should be paved first?
The first template ships and Victor asks for the exit. What belongs in a template?
A security fix reaches nine of thirty pipelines. How does a template stay alive after copying?
Kofi wants to skip the weekly review, and Marcus agrees. Can guardrails replace a gate?
Asha wants one number that proves the golden path works. Which number shows teams chose it?
Next week: four hundred people can see rider phone numbers. Which columns hold personal data?
modules.boss: The weekend review: nobody uses our templates. Decide which journey to pave, what the template sets by default, how it stays current, which checks move into CI, and which metric shows teams chose it.
modules.finale: Nine of twelve new pipelines now start from the path, and Victor's team ships one too. Grace says, 'Make the right way the easy way.' Then Lena finds rider phone numbers in a dashboard four hundred people can open.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why don't people just do it your way?" Marcus: "Because we made our way the easiest one, so now most of them want to."

modules.logline: Rider phone numbers in an open dashboard push Marcus to build governance that protects riders without slowing the teams that need the data.
scenes: Four hundred people can see rider phone numbers in a Lumen dashboard. Nobody has misused them. Legal wants every dashboard locked. Kofi says locking everything stops the business. What is governance for, if not for saying no?

Marcus asks how many columns hold personal data. Nobody knows: names, emails, drop-off coordinates, a free-text notes field. Victor suggests tagging by hand. Lena counts eleven thousand columns. Can classification run automatically, and how accurate must it be?

Support needs a rider's phone number for an open ticket, in their own city only. Roles alone would mean forty new roles. Victor proposes attributes and row rules. How do roles, attributes and policies combine without becoming unmanageable?

Data scientists need to join trips to riders without seeing who the riders are. Masking breaks the join; Victor suggests tokenisation; legal asks about pseudonymisation. Three words that sound alike. Which one protects riders and keeps the join?

A column tagged personal in Snowflake loses its tag after one Delta transform. Meanwhile legal puts a hold on Chennai trips that retention rules want deleted. Which rule wins, and how does lineage carry a tag downstream?

The auditors arrive on Monday and ask for evidence: who accessed rider data, under which policy, approved by whom. Victor's team keeps policies in a wiki. Marcus keeps them in code. Which one survives an audit?
teasers: Eleven thousand columns and nobody knows which are personal. Can classification run automatically?
One phone number would need forty new roles. How do roles, attributes and policies combine?
Scientists must join riders to trips without knowing who they are. Which technique keeps the join?
A personal-data tag vanishes after one transform. How does lineage carry a tag downstream?
Auditors arrive Monday and the policies live in a wiki. Which kind of policy survives an audit?
Next week: nobody can say what the platform team does. What would a service level promise?
modules.boss: The weekend review: the phone-number dashboard. Show how the column escaped classification, which policy should have masked it, how lineage would have carried the tag, and what evidence you would hand the auditors.
modules.finale: The audit closes with no findings, and teams barely notice the new rules. Victor moves Lumen's wiki into code without being asked. Grace says, 'Good governance is the kind people forget is there.' Then Asha asks what the platform is for.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why can't everyone see everything?" Marcus: "Some things are private, like your diary, so only people who really need them get the key."

modules.logline: Running the merged platform as a product puts Marcus and Victor side by side on service levels, cost and adoption, until Asha must choose one of them to lead it.
scenes: Asha merges both teams into one data platform and gives Marcus and Victor a quarter to prove it is worth funding. Tom asks what the platform team actually does. Neither has a crisp answer. Who are its users, really?

Marcus proposes SLOs: trips fresh by 6 a.m. on 99.5% of days. Victor wants 99.9%. Lena asks what happens when the error budget runs out in week two. Does the team stop shipping features, or keep going?

A Snowflake outage hits during the finance close. Lena runs the incident well, but forty teams learn of it from Kofi. Victor says the fix mattered more than the updates. How should a platform team communicate during an incident?

Mei brings the bill: the merged platform costs more than both did apart, and nobody knows which team spends what. She wants showback by Friday. Victor fears it starts a turf war. What is the right unit cost for a trip?

Victor shows active users rising. Marcus shows time to a trusted number falling from five days to one. Tom brings fourteen roadmap requests and wants all of them. Which metric shows outcomes, and how do they say no?

Asha asks for one page each: how the platform team should be funded, shaped and staffed for two years. Marcus and Victor draft separately, then compare. The pages are nearly identical. So why must Asha still pick one?
teasers: 99.5% against 99.9%, and an error budget runs out. Does the team stop shipping features?
Snowflake fails during close and forty teams hear it from Kofi. How should a platform team communicate?
Mei wants cost showback by Friday. What is the right unit cost for a trip?
Tom brings fourteen roadmap requests. Which metric shows outcomes, and how do you say no?
Two architects write one page each on the platform's future. Why must Asha still pick one?
Next week: two drafts, one CTO who reads page one. What belongs in a design doc?
modules.boss: The weekend review: Asha's quarterly platform review. Present the SLOs and error budget, the incident communication, Mei's unit cost per trip and the adoption numbers that matter. Then defend the three roadmap items you said no to.
modules.finale: The quarter closes: SLOs met, costs shown per team, adoption real. Grace says, 'The job goes to whoever makes the other one better.' Asha calls Marcus and Victor in together. She has read both decision logs and made her choice.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Is the platform a shop?" Marcus: "Sort of; our customers are the other teams, and we only win if they want to come back."
